presentation: Suspected infectious pulmonary tuberculosis: infection control
stem:
A 47-year-old man with no fixed address attends the emergency department with seven weeks of productive cough, drenching night sweats and marked weight loss. A chest X-ray shows cavitation in the right upper zone. He is haemodynamically stable but cannot be safely discharged, so he is admitted to a medical ward.

Which arrangement is most appropriate to limit spread of infection to other patients?

options.A: A bed in an open bay near the nurses' station so that he can be closely observed
options.B: A shared bay with other patients who also have a persistent cough, to cohort them together
options.C: A single room with the door propped open so that nurses can observe him easily
options.D: A single room with the door kept closed and early sputum samples sent to the laboratory
options.E: Any available bed with the curtains drawn and staff wearing plastic aprons only

correct_answer: D. A single room with the door kept closed and early sputum samples sent to the laboratory
why_correct: A long cough with night sweats, weight loss and upper-zone cavitation is pulmonary tuberculosis until proved otherwise, and it spreads by the airborne route through inhaled droplet nuclei. NICE advises that people with suspected infectious pulmonary TB who stay in hospital are cared for in a single room as a minimum (a negative pressure room if they are at high risk of multidrug-resistant TB), and that several respiratory samples are sent for microscopy and culture so that the diagnosis and drug resistance can be established. Keeping the door closed is standard infection-control practice, because a single room only protects others if it is kept shut. Source: NICE NG33, Tuberculosis, 2016 (updated 2019).
why_wrong: A. An open bay exposes other patients, some of whom may be vulnerable, and closeness to the nurses' station does not reduce airborne spread. B. Cohorting people on the basis of cough alone mixes those who may not have TB with an infectious patient. C. A single room only works if the door is closed, so leaving it open defeats the purpose of isolation. E. A curtain is not a barrier to airborne particles, and an apron does not protect against inhaled droplet nuclei.
pearl: Suspected infectious pulmonary TB needs a single room with the door closed, and negative pressure only when multidrug resistance is likely.
thinking: Cavitating upper-zone lesion with night sweats and weight loss  ↓  Suspect infectious pulmonary TB  ↓  Airborne spread, so the barrier must be a closed room  ↓  Single room, door shut, early sputum samples
exam_trap: Options that keep the patient visible or nearby for observation tempt candidates away from the closed single room that actually protects others.
takeaway: Treat suspected infectious pulmonary TB as airborne: isolate in a single room with the door closed and send sputum early.
notes: New vignette (homeless admission, cavitation, ward arrangement) with the same learning point as UN1573 (respiratory isolation for suspected infectious TB). Source options 'urgent specialist assessment' and 'routine chest clinic within 3 months' replaced by ward-arrangement options. Wording follows NICE NG33 (single room as a minimum; negative pressure for high MDR risk; admission only where there is a clinical or public health need, e.g. homelessness). Bank check: no live question on TB isolation (PAN10103 is transmission route, BX422 and DT120 investigation, RES023 treatment). Options matched in length so key is neither longest nor shortest.
sources: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng33/chapter/Recommendations (fetched; recs 1.5.1.x on single room and negative pressure)

stem:
A 27-year-old woman accepts an HIV test at a walk-in sexual health outreach session. A rapid finger-prick point-of-care test is reactive. She feels well and asks anxiously whether this means she definitely has HIV.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.A: Take blood for confirmatory laboratory testing and arrange prompt HIV specialist review
options.B: Explain that HIV is definitely present and book a routine GP appointment for next month
options.C: Start antiretroviral therapy from the outreach session so that treatment is not delayed at all
options.D: Advise her to repeat the same finger-prick test in three months and take no other action
options.E: Contact her workplace and sexual contacts so that they can arrange testing straight away

correct_answer: A. Take blood for confirmatory laboratory testing and arrange prompt HIV specialist review
why_correct: Point-of-care tests have reduced specificity and sensitivity compared with fourth-generation laboratory tests, so false positives occur and a reactive result needs confirmation by serological testing. NICE advises that people who test positive are then seen by an HIV specialist, preferably within 48 hours and certainly within 2 weeks. Source: NICE NG60, HIV testing: increasing uptake among people who may have undiagnosed HIV, 2016 (point-of-care testing and referral pathway recommendations).
why_wrong: B. The result is not yet diagnostic, and a routine appointment weeks later delays specialist care. C. Antiretroviral therapy is started by the HIV team after confirmation and baseline tests, not from an outreach session. D. Waiting three months leaves a possible new infection unconfirmed and untreated. E. Telling an employer or contacts without her consent breaches confidentiality, and partner notification is handled by the sexual health team.
pearl: A reactive rapid HIV test is a screen: confirm it with a laboratory test, then refer to HIV specialists quickly.
thinking: Reactive point-of-care HIV test  ↓  Lower specificity means false positives are possible  ↓  Confirm with laboratory serology  ↓  Arrange prompt specialist HIV care with support
exam_trap: Telling the patient the diagnosis is certain, or acting on it, before confirmatory testing is complete.
takeaway: A reactive HIV screening test needs confirmation and rapid specialist follow-up, with confidentiality maintained.
notes: Rewritten as a point-of-care test scenario; no live PLAB 1 question tests confirmation of a reactive HIV screen (PAN7231 starts after confirmation; BX620 is generic screening). 'Years later' distractor replaced. NICE NG60 fetched and checked (confirmatory serology, specialist within 48 h/2 weeks).
sources: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng60/chapter/Recommendations

presentation: Negative HIV test in the window period
stem:
A 31-year-old man attends a sexual health clinic three weeks after condomless sex with a new partner whose HIV status is unknown. He has no symptoms. A fourth-generation HIV blood test today is negative, and he asks whether this means he can stop worrying and need not use condoms.

What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: The result may be negative because it is early, so he should repeat the test after the window period
options.B: The negative result proves he is uninfected, so he can stop using condoms with new partners
options.C: The negative result is a false negative, so he should wait for seroconversion symptoms before retesting
options.D: A negative laboratory test at any point means he will never need another HIV test in future
options.E: A fourth-generation test detects infection from the day of exposure, so the result is conclusive

correct_answer: A. The result may be negative because it is early, so he should repeat the test after the window period
why_correct: The window period is the time between exposure and when a test can reliably detect infection. A negative result within it does not exclude HIV, so the patient should be offered a repeat test once it has passed and advised to use condoms meanwhile. NICE NG60 recommends another test once people are past the window period, and describes about 1 month for fourth-generation tests. Source: NICE NG60, 2016 (amended 2025).
why_wrong: B. A negative result this early cannot prove he is uninfected, and condoms still protect him and his partners. C. The result may be accurate for now, and waiting for symptoms would miss most infections. D. Ongoing risk means ongoing repeat testing, whatever an earlier result showed. E. Even fourth-generation tests need time after exposure to turn positive, so they are not conclusive on the day.
pearl: A negative HIV test only excludes infection acquired before the window period began.
thinking: Negative test shortly after exposure  ↓  Inside the window period, so not conclusive  ↓  Advise condoms and repeat test after the window period  ↓  Explain the reason clearly
exam_trap: Reassuring the patient on an early negative result because the test is a modern fourth-generation assay.
takeaway: A negative HIV test soon after exposure does not exclude infection, so explain the window period and plan a repeat test.
notes: Fixed 3-week interval chosen so the 72-hour PEP window is not in play. NICE NG60 page (fetched) gives the window as about 1 month for fourth-generation tests; BASHH may allow a longer interval for some assays, so the stem uses a duration clearly inside any window. No live PLAB 1 question tests this (ID002 is a seroconversion illness with PCR). Source distractor 'repeat if symptoms develop' kept in changed form (C).
sources: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng60/chapter/Recommendations

stem:
A 29-year-old woman who is 30 weeks pregnant returns from six weeks in rural South Asia, where she drank untreated well water. Over four days she develops nausea, dark urine and jaundice, with a tender liver edge and markedly raised transaminases. She has no tattoos, transfusions or injecting drug use, and her partner is well.

Which infection is of particular concern because it can cause severe liver disease in her situation?

options.A: Hepatitis E virus infection
options.B: Hepatitis C virus infection
options.C: Cytomegalovirus infection
options.D: Epstein-Barr virus infection
options.E: Hepatitis D virus co-infection with hepatitis B

correct_answer: A. Hepatitis E virus infection
why_correct: Hepatitis E is spread by the faecal-oral route through contaminated water or food and is common in parts of Asia and Africa. It is usually self-limiting, but in pregnancy, especially the third trimester, infection with the genotypes seen in endemic regions carries a much higher risk of fulminant liver failure and poor fetal outcomes. Source: standard UK teaching on travel-associated viral hepatitis in pregnancy (British Liver Trust, Hepatitis E and pregnancy).
why_wrong: B. Hepatitis C is blood-borne, usually causes a silent infection and has no risk factors here. C. Cytomegalovirus rarely causes marked jaundice in an immunocompetent adult and has no link to untreated water. D. Epstein-Barr virus causes sore throat and lymphadenopathy, with only mild liver enzyme changes. E. Hepatitis D needs hepatitis B to replicate and is spread by blood or sexual contact, not by water.
pearl: Hepatitis E behaves like hepatitis A in transmission but carries a far higher risk of severe disease in pregnancy.
thinking: Pregnant, travelled, unsafe water, acute hepatitis  ↓  Faecal-oral virus rather than blood-borne virus  ↓  Hepatitis E is the one with severe pregnancy complications  ↓  Hepatitis E
exam_trap: Choosing a blood-borne or herpes virus because the picture looks like any acute hepatitis, and missing the water exposure and the pregnancy.
takeaway: In a pregnant traveller with acute hepatitis after unsafe water, think of hepatitis E because of its risk of fulminant disease.
notes: PAN2488 and PAN6648 share one learning point (hepatitis E in pregnancy); no live PLAB 1 question tests it (searched HEV, hepatitis E, ribavirin); PAN6648 skipped as same point. Source distractors with 'only' removed; hepatitis A omitted from options to avoid ambiguity. Not verified against a fetched UKHSA page (gov.uk URL 404, nhs.uk blank); content is standard teaching.
sources: Carried over from AKT source; standard teaching (UKHSA/WHO hepatitis E), page not fetched

presentation: Lumbar puncture in suspected meningitis with raised ICP signs
stem:
A 41-year-old man attends the emergency department with a day of fever, headache and neck stiffness. He becomes increasingly drowsy, develops weakness of his left arm and has unequal pupils. Bacterial meningitis is suspected, blood cultures are taken and intravenous antibiotics are given. The registrar decides to arrange brain imaging before any lumbar puncture.

What is the main reason for holding the lumbar puncture?

options.A: The needle could introduce infection into cerebrospinal fluid that is already inflamed
options.B: A blood-stained traumatic tap would make the cell count impossible to interpret properly
options.C: Removing fluid could cause brain herniation when intracranial pressure is raised
options.D: The new weakness means the diagnosis is now encephalitis, so the fluid will not help
options.E: Post-dural puncture headache would worsen his already depressed conscious level

correct_answer: C. Removing fluid could cause brain herniation when intracranial pressure is raised
why_correct: New focal neurological signs, abnormal pupils or a falling level of consciousness suggest raised intracranial pressure or a space-occupying lesion. Removing cerebrospinal fluid in that setting risks brain herniation (coning), so imaging comes first and lumbar puncture is delayed. Antibiotics must not wait for either test. Source: NICE NG240, Meningitis (bacterial) and meningococcal disease, 2024, recommendation 1.4.12.
why_wrong: A. Meningitis is already present, and the concern is pressure rather than introducing infection. B. A traumatic tap can blur results but is not a reason to withhold the test. D. Focal signs can occur with bacterial meningitis and its complications, and do not establish encephalitis. E. Headache after puncture is a minor, treatable effect and not a contraindication.
pearl: Focal signs, abnormal pupils or a falling conscious level mean imaging before lumbar puncture, while antibiotics are never delayed.
thinking: Suspected meningitis with focal signs and falling consciousness  ↓  Possible raised intracranial pressure  ↓  Lumbar puncture risks herniation  ↓  Give antibiotics now and image before any puncture
exam_trap: Delaying antibiotics while waiting for imaging or lumbar puncture.
takeaway: In meningitis, signs of raised intracranial pressure contraindicate lumbar puncture because of herniation risk, but antibiotics must go ahead.
notes: Stem rebuilt as an ED case with drowsiness, arm weakness and pupil asymmetry, aligned to NICE NG240 1.4.12 (fetched). No GCS number used. Checked live bank: no meningitis question tests why LP is delayed (DF001 is brain abscess, PMG026 is IIH papilloedema).
sources: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng240/chapter/Recommendations

stem:
A 7-year-old girl is brought to her GP two weeks after being scratched on the forearm by a new kitten. A small red papule has formed at the scratch, and she now has a tender, 3 cm lump in her right axilla with a low-grade temperature. She is otherwise well and has not been bitten.

Which organism is the most likely cause?

options.A: Pasteurella multocida, a Gram-negative coccobacillus
options.B: Toxoplasma gondii, an intracellular protozoan
options.C: Staphylococcus aureus, a Gram-positive coccus
options.D: Epstein-Barr virus, a herpesvirus
options.E: Bartonella henselae, a Gram-negative bacillus

correct_answer: E. Bartonella henselae, a Gram-negative bacillus
why_correct: Cat-scratch disease is caused by Bartonella henselae, transmitted by a scratch or bite from a cat, usually a kitten. A papule appears at the inoculation site and tender regional lymphadenopathy follows within weeks. The illness is usually self-limiting. Source: standard UK teaching (UKHSA/NHS pages not accessed for this item).
why_wrong: A. Pasteurella multocida causes rapid cellulitis within hours of a bite, not a delayed node. B. Toxoplasma gondii is acquired from cat faeces or undercooked meat and typically causes cervical nodes without an inoculation papule. C. Staphylococcus aureus tends to cause an abscess or cellulitis rather than a delayed regional node. D. Epstein-Barr virus causes generalised lymphadenopathy with sore throat, not a node proximal to a scratch.
pearl: A scratch papule followed by regional lymph-node swelling points to Bartonella henselae.
thinking: Kitten scratch  ↓  Papule at the scratch site  ↓  Regional lymphadenopathy two weeks later  ↓  Bartonella henselae
exam_trap: Choosing Pasteurella because of the cat, when its picture is a rapid cellulitis after a bite.
takeaway: Cat-scratch disease is caused by Bartonella henselae and presents as regional lymphadenopathy after a scratch.
notes: Pasteurella and Toxoplasma replace unrelated source distractors (tetanus, malaria, syphilis, Lyme) so options are plausible cat-related organisms. No live PLAB 1 question tests Bartonella (searched Bartonella, cat scratch, lymphadenopathy with cat). Not verified against a fetched page (nhs.uk blank); standard teaching.
sources: Carried over from AKT source; standard teaching, page not fetched

stem:
A 44-year-old man attends the emergency department with two days of double vision, drooping eyelids, a dry mouth and slurred speech. This morning he choked on a drink and his shoulders and arms now feel weak. He has no fever, is fully alert and has normal sensation. His pupils are dilated and react sluggishly. Three days ago he ate home-canned vegetables at a family gathering, and two relatives have similar symptoms.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Guillain–Barré syndrome
options.B: Myasthenia gravis in crisis
options.C: Brainstem ischaemic stroke
options.D: Generalised tetanus infection
options.E: Foodborne botulism poisoning

correct_answer: E. Foodborne botulism poisoning
why_correct: Botulinum neurotoxin blocks acetylcholine release at the neuromuscular junction, causing symmetrical cranial nerve palsies and autonomic features (dilated pupils, dry mouth) followed by descending flaccid paralysis in an alert, afebrile patient with normal sensation. A cluster of cases after home-preserved food makes foodborne botulism the diagnosis. Suspected cases need urgent senior and ITU input, early discussion with the UKHSA Botulism Service about antitoxin, and notification to the health protection team. Source: UKHSA, Botulism: clinical and public health management (guidance page fetched).
why_wrong: A. Guillain–Barré syndrome typically ascends from the legs with sensory symptoms and absent reflexes, usually after an infection, and does not cause a dilated pupil with a dry mouth. B. Myasthenia gravis causes fatiguable weakness with spared pupils and does not cluster after a shared meal. C. A brainstem stroke would give asymmetrical or crossed signs with sudden onset rather than symmetrical bulbar and arm weakness in several people. D. Tetanus causes muscle rigidity and spasms, not flaccid paralysis, and follows a contaminated wound.
pearl: Botulism is the cause of descending (not ascending) symmetrical flaccid paralysis that starts with the eyes and throat.
thinking: Alert, afebrile adult with bilateral cranial nerve signs, dry mouth and dilated pupils  ↓  Weakness spreads from the face and throat down to the arms, sensation normal  ↓  Home-preserved food and others unwell make a toxin illness likely  ↓  Foodborne botulism
exam_trap: Guillain–Barré syndrome is tempting as a cause of acute flaccid weakness, but it ascends, is sensory and does not cause a dilated pupil or a shared-food cluster.
takeaway: Eye and throat weakness that descends in a clear-minded patient after home-preserved food is botulism until proven otherwise.
notes: Same learning point as source (foodborne botulism). New vignette adds dilated pupils, dry mouth and a family cluster to differentiate from GBS and myasthenia; explanation expanded with UKHSA antitoxin/notification. No botulism question in live bank.
sources: https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/botulism-clinical-and-public-health-management

presentation: Snuffles and palm-sole rash in an infant
stem:
A 5-week-old boy is brought to the GP with a persistent blood-stained nasal discharge and noisy breathing that has not improved with saline drops. He has a coppery rash on his palms and soles, a palpable liver and spleen, and is feeding poorly. His mother moved to the UK late in pregnancy and had no antenatal blood tests.

Which untreated maternal infection best explains these findings?

options.A: Treponema pallidum infection
options.B: Rubella virus infection
options.C: Toxoplasma gondii infection
options.D: Cytomegalovirus infection
options.E: Varicella-zoster virus infection

correct_answer: A. Treponema pallidum infection
why_correct: Treponema pallidum crosses the placenta, and untreated maternal syphilis causes congenital syphilis. Early features include persistent nasal discharge (snuffles), a rash involving the palms and soles, hepatosplenomegaly and bone changes, and later features include dental and skeletal abnormalities. Antenatal screening and treatment of the mother is the means of prevention. Source: NHS syphilis guidance (congenital syphilis) and UK antenatal infectious diseases screening programme, with standard paediatric teaching.
why_wrong: B. Congenital rubella classically causes cataracts, sensorineural deafness and congenital heart disease rather than snuffles and a palm-sole rash. C. Congenital toxoplasmosis causes chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus and intracranial calcification. D. Congenital cytomegalovirus causes microcephaly, petechiae and hearing loss, not nasal discharge with a coppery palm and sole rash. E. Congenital varicella causes limb scarring and hypoplasia and eye damage after maternal infection early in pregnancy.
pearl: Snuffles plus a rash on the palms and soles in a young infant should prompt a syphilis serology request.
thinking: Young infant with bloody nasal discharge, palm-sole rash and hepatosplenomegaly  ↓  Mother had no antenatal screening  ↓  Features fit congenital syphilis rather than the other congenital infections  ↓  Treponema pallidum infection
exam_trap: Congenital infections are often grouped together, but only syphilis gives snuffles with a palm and sole rash and bone involvement.
takeaway: Untreated maternal syphilis causes congenital syphilis; antenatal screening prevents it.
notes: Same learning point as source (congenital syphilis from untreated maternal infection); source stem was a vague nasal-discharge/dental vignette with implausible distractors, now an early-infant presentation with classic snuffles and rash and plausible congenital-infection distractors. Late dental signs mentioned only in explanation. No congenital syphilis question live.
sources: Standard teaching (UKHSA antenatal infectious diseases screening; BASHH syphilis guidance) - not fetched

stem:
A 24-year-old woman is diagnosed with pelvic inflammatory disease at a sexual health clinic and is given antibiotics. Swabs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea have been sent and results are awaited. She has had two sexual partners in the last three months and is currently with one of them.

Which action is an essential part of her management?

options.A: Ask her to tell her current partner to see his own GP only if he later develops symptoms
options.B: Hold any discussion about her partners until her own swab results are available
options.C: Offer recent partners testing and treatment for chlamydia and gonorrhoea even if well
options.D: Advise a week of abstinence and then discharge her with no further follow-up
options.E: Offer treatment to a partner only if he reports urethral discharge or dysuria

correct_answer: C. Offer recent partners testing and treatment for chlamydia and gonorrhoea even if well
why_correct: PID is usually caused by sexually transmitted organisms, so her current partner should be contacted and offered testing and treatment for chlamydia and gonorrhoea, and other recent partners (traced back about six months from the onset of her symptoms) may be offered the same, without waiting for her results. This matters because many infected male partners have no symptoms, and it prevents reinfection and onward transmission. She should also avoid sex until she and her partners have completed treatment. Source: BASHH UK national guideline for the management of pelvic inflammatory disease (2018, updated 2019).
why_wrong: A. Waiting for symptoms misses asymptomatic infection, which is common in men. B. Delaying partner contact until results return leaves infected partners untreated and risks reinfection. D. A week of abstinence is not enough, and she needs follow-up to confirm response and complete screening. E. Treating only symptomatic partners leaves asymptomatic infected partners untreated.
pearl: In PID, partner notification and treatment is part of the treatment of the patient, not an optional extra.
thinking: PID is usually a sexually acquired infection  ↓  Partners may carry infection without symptoms  ↓  Trace, test and treat recent partners without delay  ↓  Offer recent partners testing and treatment for chlamydia and gonorrhoea
exam_trap: Partner management is often left until results are back or limited to symptomatic partners, which allows reinfection.
takeaway: Always arrange partner notification and treatment for recent partners when managing PID.
notes: Same learning point as source (partner testing and treatment is essential in sexually acquired PID); source's wrong single-dose azithromycin option replaced. Live partner-notification questions are for chlamydia/gonorrhoea (ID031, ID045, BX994), not PID; moderate overlap risk, reviewer may prefer skip. Key claim (partners within about 6 months tested/treated without awaiting results) per BASHH PID 2019 from memory - not fetched.
sources: Standard teaching (BASHH PID guideline 2019; not fetched)

stem:
An 18-year-old university student attends an out-of-hours GP service with five days of stinging on passing urine and needing to pass urine often. A urine dipstick shows white cells but no nitrites and no blood. Over the last two days she has also had a dull ache low in her abdomen, a new yellow vaginal discharge and pain deep inside during sex. She feels hot and shivery. On examination both sides of the pelvis are tender and moving the cervix is very painful. She had condomless sex with a new partner three weeks ago.

Which diagnosis is most likely?

options.A: Lower urinary tract infection
options.B: Acute pyelonephritis
options.C: Pelvic inflammatory disease
options.D: Vulvovaginal candidiasis
options.E: Ruptured ovarian cyst

correct_answer: C. Pelvic inflammatory disease
why_correct: Dysuria and frequency can occur with pelvic inflammatory disease, but lower abdominal pain, deep dyspareunia, abnormal discharge, fever and cervical motion and adnexal tenderness in a sexually active young woman point to PID, and white cells without nitrites do not make this a urinary infection. Empirical treatment should start without waiting for swab results, alongside a pregnancy test and chlamydia and gonorrhoea NAATs. Source: BASHH, UK national guideline for the management of pelvic inflammatory disease, 2019.
why_wrong: A. A simple lower urinary tract infection does not cause discharge, deep dyspareunia or cervical motion tenderness, and the dipstick lacks nitrites. B. Pyelonephritis gives loin pain, rigors and a higher fever rather than pelvic tenderness. D. Candidiasis causes itching and a thick white discharge without pelvic tenderness or fever. E. A ruptured cyst causes sudden severe pain, usually without fever or discharge.
pearl: Do not stop at cystitis when urinary symptoms come with discharge and pelvic tenderness.
thinking: Urinary symptoms plus discharge, deep dyspareunia and low-grade fever  ↓  Negative nitrites, cervical motion and adnexal tenderness  ↓  Pelvic infection from a sexually acquired organism  ↓  Pelvic inflammatory disease
exam_trap: Urinary symptoms attract the label cystitis, but a discharge and pelvic tenderness on examination point elsewhere.
takeaway: Think PID when dysuria accompanies discharge, pelvic pain and cervical motion tenderness.
notes: Same learning point as source (PID can present with urinary symptoms plus discharge/pelvic pain). Live PID questions (ID033, OG038, DS044, DS045, PAQ14787, BX873) test treatment, investigations or the classic presentation; this urinary-mimic angle is not tested, but diagnosis overlaps PAQ14787/OG038 somewhat. Management detail kept in explanation only.
sources: Standard teaching (BASHH PID guideline 2019; not fetched)

stem:
A 68-year-old man develops fever, shaking chills and a cough productive of rust-coloured sputum over 24 hours. He has sharp right-sided chest pain on breathing in. A chest X-ray shows consolidation confined to the right lower lobe. He has no recent travel, hospital admission or exposure to others who are unwell.

Which organism most commonly causes this community-acquired pneumonia?

options.A: Legionella pneumophila
options.B: Klebsiella pneumoniae
options.C: Staphylococcus aureus
options.D: Streptococcus pneumoniae
options.E: Mycoplasma pneumoniae (atypical)

correct_answer: D. Streptococcus pneumoniae
why_correct: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the commonest cause of community-acquired pneumonia in adults, classically presenting with abrupt fever, pleuritic chest pain, rust-coloured sputum and lobar consolidation. Severity is then assessed with a score such as CURB65 and empirical antibiotics follow local guidance. Source: NICE NG250, Pneumonia: diagnosis and management, 2025 (severity assessment); the organism is standard teaching.
why_wrong: A. Legionella usually follows exposure to contaminated water systems and often has diarrhoea and confusion. B. Klebsiella is associated with alcohol excess or diabetes and thick, blood-stained sputum. C. Staphylococcus aureus pneumonia typically follows influenza and causes cavitation. E. Mycoplasma causes a gradual illness in younger adults with a dry cough and chest X-ray changes out of keeping with the examination.
pearl: Abrupt onset, pleuritic pain, rust-coloured sputum and a lobar shadow in a community patient is pneumococcal until shown otherwise.
thinking: Acute febrile illness with pleuritic pain and rusty sputum  ↓  Lobar consolidation, no special exposure or risk factor  ↓  Commonest community pathogen fitting this picture is pneumococcus  ↓  Streptococcus pneumoniae
exam_trap: Legionella and atypicals attract attention in exams, but without a water-system exposure, extrapulmonary features or a dry cough, the common organism is still the answer.
takeaway: Streptococcus pneumoniae is the commonest cause of community-acquired pneumonia.
notes: Same learning point as source (S. pneumoniae commonest CAP organism). Source was a bare one-line recall with implausible distractors; built vignette with plausible organism distractors. Live bank checked: pneumococcus as the CAP organism not tested elsewhere (BX936, ID019 test treatment/severity).
sources: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng250
Standard teaching - organism frequency not quoted from the page

stem:
A 5-year-old boy has had two days of sore throat and fever, followed by a widespread rash that feels like sandpaper. The GP diagnoses scarlet fever and prescribes phenoxymethylpenicillin. His father asks when the boy can go back to school.

What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Return to school as soon as the rash has started to fade
options.B: Stay at home until the whole course of antibiotics has been completed
options.C: Stay at home until a repeat throat swab culture has come back negative
options.D: Stay at home for two weeks from the date on which the rash first appeared
options.E: Stay at home until at least 24 hours after starting the antibiotic

correct_answer: E. Stay at home until at least 24 hours after starting the antibiotic
why_correct: Scarlet fever is a notifiable group A streptococcal infection, so the GP should notify the local health protection team. UKHSA advises that children and staff stay away from school, nursery or work until at least 24 hours after starting appropriate antibiotics. Routine antibiotic prophylaxis for household contacts is not recommended. Source: UKHSA, Guidelines for the public health management of scarlet fever outbreaks (2023) (PDF fetched).
why_wrong: A. Fading of the rash does not mark the end of infectiousness; antibiotics do. B. Waiting for the whole course to finish keeps him out of school for far longer than necessary. C. Repeat throat swabs are not required to clear a child to return. D. A fixed two weeks has no basis in current guidance.
pearl: The exclusion period for scarlet fever is counted from the first antibiotic dose, not from the rash or the end of treatment.
thinking: Clinical scarlet fever and treatment started  ↓  Question concerns infectivity and public health  ↓  24 hours of effective antibiotics, then return  ↓  Stay at home until at least 24 hours after starting the antibiotic
exam_trap: Candidates may choose to wait until the rash fades or the course ends, but guidance ties return to 24 hours after the first dose.
takeaway: For scarlet fever, notify the health protection team and exclude until 24 hours after antibiotics start.
notes: Same learning point family as source (scarlet fever is infectious, apply public-health measures); source key was vague so re-angled to the concrete UKHSA exclusion rule (24 hours after starting antibiotics) and notification. 24-hour rule is stable, not a movable threshold. No live scarlet fever public-health question (PAQ16392/PED022/BX908 test diagnosis only).
sources: https://assets.publishing.service.gov.uk/media/6426e4f1fbe620000c17da7e/guidelines-for-public-health-management-scarlet-fever-outbreaks-january-2023_.pdf

stem:
A 5-year-old girl has chickenpox, with a mixture of fresh blisters and scabbed spots. Her mother asks how to protect other people while she is infectious. Two regular visitors worry her: the girl's grandmother, who is having chemotherapy, and a neighbour who is 20 weeks pregnant and is not sure whether she has ever had chickenpox.

What is the most appropriate advice?

options.A: Visits can carry on once the girl's temperature has settled and she feels well in herself
options.B: Contact is safe with careful handwashing, since chickenpox spreads only by direct skin contact
options.C: Give both women oral aciclovir now as routine prophylaxis, before any contact has happened
options.D: Keep her away from both women until every spot has scabbed over, and tell them to seek advice
options.E: Stop visits only if the grandmother develops a rash, as pregnant women are at no particular risk

correct_answer: D. Keep her away from both women until every spot has scabbed over, and tell them to seek advice
why_correct: Chickenpox can be severe in pregnancy, in newborns and in people with weakened immunity, so contact with these groups should be avoided while the child is infectious, until all the spots have formed scabs. A non-immune pregnant woman or an immunosuppressed person who has been in contact should seek urgent medical advice, as prophylaxis may be offered. Source: NHS, Chickenpox, 2025.
why_wrong: A. Infectiousness continues until the last spots have crusted, whether or not the fever has settled. B. The virus spreads by airborne droplets as well as by contact with blister fluid, so handwashing alone is not enough. C. Aciclovir is not given as routine prophylaxis before exposure; it is considered after significant exposure in those at risk. E. Pregnant women who are not immune are at risk of serious complications, so they are not exempt from the advice.
pearl: Infectiousness lasts until every lesion has crusted, and vulnerable contacts should be kept away until then.
thinking: Child with active chickenpox  ↓  Visitors include an immunosuppressed woman and a possibly non-immune pregnant woman  ↓  Avoid contact until all lesions are scabbed and advise exposed vulnerable contacts to seek advice
exam_trap: Judging infectiousness by the fever alone instead of the state of the lesions.
takeaway: Keep children with active chickenpox away from pregnant, newborn and immunosuppressed people until the lesions have crusted.
notes: Source key retained; the old distractors (aciclovir for siblings, shared towels, isolate until fever settles) rebuilt. Live BX771 tests the infectious period only and ID018/DS093/DR110 test management after an exposure; none tests the advice to keep an infectious child away from vulnerable contacts. School-return rule dropped (not verified). Fetched nhs.uk chickenpox page.
sources: https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/chickenpox/

stem:
A 31-year-old man has had a sore throat for two days, with no cough. He is otherwise well and has no features of serious illness. After assessing him, his GP decides that antibiotics are not needed immediately but that a back-up prescription is reasonable.

What advice should the GP give about the prescription?

options.A: Start the antibiotic straight away and stop it as soon as the throat feels better
options.B: Take it from the first day, because antibiotics shorten a sore throat by several days
options.C: Keep it in reserve for future sore throats so that treatment can start earlier next time
options.D: Use it if symptoms have not begun to improve within a few days or get markedly worse
options.E: Use it only if the sore throat comes back within a few weeks of settling down

correct_answer: D. Use it if symptoms have not begun to improve within a few days or get markedly worse
why_correct: A back-up (delayed) prescription is for people who probably do not need an antibiotic straight away. The patient should be told that an antibiotic is not needed immediately, to use the prescription if symptoms have not started to improve within a few days or worsen rapidly or significantly, and to seek medical help if they become systemically very unwell. Source: NICE NG84, Sore throat (acute): antimicrobial prescribing, 2018 (recommendation 1.1.9).
why_wrong: A. Starting it at once defeats the purpose of a back-up prescription, and the advice is not to stop as soon as he feels better. B. Antibiotics shorten a sore throat only slightly, by hours rather than days, and most people improve within a week without them. C. It is for this illness only, and keeping antibiotics for later episodes encourages inappropriate use and resistance. E. The prescription relates to the current illness failing to improve or worsening, not to a recurrence weeks later.
pearl: A back-up prescription comes with instructions: when to use it and when to seek urgent help.
thinking: Self-limiting sore throat, antibiotic not needed now  ↓  Back-up prescription agreed  ↓  Explain the trigger for using it (no improvement or marked worsening) plus a safety net for serious illness
exam_trap: Handing over a back-up prescription with no explanation of when to use it turns it into an immediate prescription.
takeaway: A back-up prescription needs clear instructions about when to use it and when to seek urgent help.
notes: Source is a bare one-line stewardship item; rebuilt as a sore-throat vignette using the NICE back-up wording (3 to 5 days / worsens rapidly or significantly), softened to 'a few days'. Live PAN9938/BX968/PAQ14840 teach declining antibiotics for viral URTI; PMG050/PAQ1065 have a back-up prescription as the key but test indication/drug, not the counselling content. No live item tests how to counsel on a back-up prescription. Fetched NG84 recommendations 1.1.4 to 1.1.9.
sources: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng84/chapter/Recommendations

presentation: Anal squamous cell carcinoma and HPV
stem:
A 52-year-old man living with HIV has had several months of anal bleeding and discomfort on opening his bowels. Examination shows a firm ulcerated lesion at the anal margin, and biopsy confirms squamous cell carcinoma.

Which infection is most strongly associated with the development of this cancer?

options.A: Persistent human papillomavirus infection
options.B: Chronic hepatitis B virus infection
options.C: Recurrent genital herpes simplex infection
options.D: Previous Epstein–Barr virus infection
options.E: Long-standing Helicobacter pylori infection

correct_answer: A. Persistent human papillomavirus infection
why_correct: Most anal squamous cell carcinomas are caused by persistent infection with high-risk types of human papillomavirus, in the same way as cervical cancer. Risk is higher in people living with HIV and in men who have sex with men, who are therefore prioritised for HPV vaccination through sexual health services. Source: UKHSA Green Book, human papillomavirus chapter; standard teaching.
why_wrong: B. Hepatitis B is linked to hepatocellular carcinoma, not anal cancer. C. Genital herpes causes recurrent painful ulcers but is not a recognised cause of anal carcinoma. D. Epstein–Barr virus is associated with Burkitt lymphoma and nasopharyngeal carcinoma. E. Helicobacter pylori is associated with gastric adenocarcinoma and MALT lymphoma.
pearl: The oncogenic HPV types behind cervical cancer also cause most anal, penile and many oropharyngeal cancers.
thinking: Anal squamous cell carcinoma confirmed  ↓  Name the virus linked to anogenital squamous cancers  ↓  HPV, with HIV as a further risk factor
exam_trap: Choosing a herpes virus because the lesion is an anal ulcer rather than recalling the oncogenic virus.
takeaway: Persistent high-risk HPV infection is the main cause of anal squamous cell carcinoma.
notes: Source is a one-liner; built into a vignette with HIV as risk context. No live item tests anal cancer or its HPV link (GF060 is penile; cervical screening items test other points). Not fetched; cited as standard teaching.
sources: Standard teaching; UKHSA Green Book HPV chapter (not fetched)

presentation: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis after sexual exposure
stem:
A 28-year-old man attends a walk-in centre on Saturday morning. The previous night he had condomless receptive anal sex with a casual male partner whose HIV status is unknown. He feels well and asks whether anything can be done to lower his chance of infection.

What is the most appropriate action?

options.A: Plan an HIV test at a routine appointment, since nothing can prevent infection after exposure
options.B: Give a single dose of an antibiotic, which prevents HIV transmission after one exposure
options.C: Arrange same-day assessment for post-exposure prophylaxis at a sexual health clinic or ED
options.D: Ask him to return if he develops a fever or rash suggesting seroconversion illness
options.E: Reassure him that one exposure carries negligible risk, so no action is needed

correct_answer: C. Arrange same-day assessment for post-exposure prophylaxis at a sexual health clinic or ED
why_correct: HIV post-exposure prophylaxis after sexual exposure (PEPSE) works best when started as soon as possible after the exposure, so he should be assessed urgently, on the same day, rather than waiting for a routine appointment. The decision depends on the type of exposure and the likelihood that the partner has HIV, and a baseline HIV test is taken with follow-up testing afterwards. Out of hours, this means a sexual health clinic or emergency department. Source: BHIVA/BASHH, UK guideline for the use of HIV post-exposure prophylaxis, 2021.
why_wrong: A. Antiretroviral drugs started promptly after exposure can prevent infection, and delay reduces their effect. B. Antibiotics have no activity against HIV. D. Waiting for seroconversion illness loses the period in which prevention is possible. E. A single condomless anal exposure carries a recognised risk, so reassurance alone is inappropriate.
pearl: PEPSE is time-critical: the sooner it starts after exposure, the better it works.
thinking: Recent significant sexual exposure, source status unknown  ↓  Prevention is still possible but time-limited  ↓  Same-day assessment for PEPSE, not routine follow-up
exam_trap: Treating a single exposure, or the absence of symptoms, as a reason to wait.
takeaway: After a significant sexual exposure to HIV, arrange urgent assessment for post-exposure prophylaxis.
notes: Source key retained, stem made specific (anal sex, unknown status). Closest live is PAQ11795 (occupational mucosal splash from a known HIV source, key = 28-day PEP course); this item tests the sexual-exposure setting and urgency of assessment, so treated as a different scenario, but checker may judge otherwise. Dose, duration and 72-hour figures deliberately omitted. BASHH PDF fetch returned HTML, so cited as standard teaching.
sources: Standard teaching; BASHH/BHIVA PEPSE guideline 2021 (not fetched)

presentation: HIV testing offer with a new STI
stem:
A 23-year-old woman is diagnosed with trichomoniasis at a sexual health clinic after changing partner recently. While waiting for her treatment, she asks whether she needs an HIV test, as she has no symptoms of HIV.

Which response is most appropriate?

options.A: An HIV test is only needed if her partner is known to come from a high-prevalence country
options.B: She should be offered an HIV test with her other tests, as a new STI signals possible risk
options.C: HIV testing should wait until her current infection has been fully treated and has cleared
options.D: Testing is advised only if she develops a flu-like illness or other signs of early HIV
options.E: Her blood can be tested for HIV without telling her, since the clinic is taking samples anyway

correct_answer: B. She should be offered an HIV test with her other tests, as a new STI signals possible risk
why_correct: A new STI shows that she has been exposed to infection and shares risk factors with HIV, so an HIV test should be offered and recommended to everyone attending for STI testing or treatment. Most people with HIV have no symptoms, and early diagnosis allows effective treatment and prevents onward spread. The test is done with her knowledge and agreement. Source: NICE NG60, HIV testing: increasing uptake among people who may have undiagnosed HIV, 2016 (recommendation 1.1.2).
why_wrong: A. Partner origin is not the criterion; risk is judged from the sexual history and the STI itself. C. There is no reason to delay testing until treatment has finished. D. Waiting for seroconversion symptoms misses most infections. E. HIV testing needs the person's knowledge and consent, even though the process is kept simple.
pearl: Offering an HIV test is a routine part of any STI assessment, not a response to high-risk labels.
thinking: New STI diagnosed in a clinic  ↓  STI and HIV share risk factors and HIV is often silent  ↓  Offer and recommend an HIV test, with her consent
exam_trap: Selecting patients for HIV testing by assumed risk group, or testing without telling them.
takeaway: Offer an HIV test, with consent, to everyone who has an STI assessment.
notes: Four near-identical source items (PAN602, PAN875, PAN1435, PAN1216) test the same point; PAN1216 is the one written, the others skipped as within-batch duplicates. PAN4854 (consent) is folded into option E and skipped. Live bank has no item for this point (BX995/PAQ15836 test STI screening in general, not the HIV offer). Fetched NG60 1.1.2.
sources: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng60/chapter/Recommendations

stem:
A 34-year-old dental hygienist has had three days of throbbing pain in her right index fingertip. She routinely examines patients' mouths, and recently did so without gloves during a busy list. The fingertip is swollen and red, with a cluster of small clear fluid-filled blisters on the pulp and a tender lump in the axilla. She has a temperature of 37.8°C and no pus can be seen or felt.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Pulp-space abscess (felon)
options.B: Herpetic whitlow
options.C: Dyshidrotic eczema (pompholyx)
options.D: Acute bacterial paronychia
options.E: Tinea manuum

correct_answer: B. Herpetic whitlow
why_correct: Grouped clear vesicles with severe pain on a swollen fingertip, after unprotected contact with oral secretions, is typical of herpetic whitlow, a herpes simplex virus infection entering through the skin. Regional lymphadenopathy and mild fever are common and there is no collection of pus. Source: standard UK clinical teaching on herpes simplex virus infection.
why_wrong: A. A felon is a tense, very tender collection of pus in the pulp space, not a cluster of clear vesicles. C. Pompholyx causes itchy, deep-seated vesicles on the sides of the fingers, usually on both hands, without an occupational exposure to herpes. D. Paronychia is a red, tender swelling of the nail fold, often with pus, and does not produce grouped vesicles. E. Tinea manuum causes a scaly, usually unilateral, slowly progressive rash rather than painful acute vesicles.
pearl: Never incise a suspected herpetic whitlow, because drainage does not help and risks secondary bacterial infection.
thinking: Painful finger after exposure to mouth secretions  ↓  grouped clear vesicles, no pus  ↓  think herpes simplex inoculation  ↓  herpetic whitlow.
exam_trap: A swollen, painful fingertip prompts surgical drainage thinking, but the clear vesicles without pus point to a viral cause.
takeaway: Grouped painful vesicles on a fingertip after contact with oral secretions mean herpetic whitlow.
notes: Original asked about a healthcare worker with painful finger vesicles after contact with an active herpes patient. Re-angled to a bare-handed dental hygienist with pulp-space abscess/paronychia contrast, adding the advice not to incise. No live PLAB question has herpetic whitlow as its answer (PAN7187 only mentions it in paronychia context).
sources: Standard teaching: no guideline page fetched

stem:
A 7-year-old boy has a sore throat and fever, and a throat swab has grown group A Streptococcus. His GP prescribes phenoxymethylpenicillin. His mother says he feels much better after three days and asks why he should keep taking the tablets.

Which is the best explanation to give her?

options.A: Finishing treatment prevents him from developing asthma later in childhood
options.B: Finishing treatment lowers the chance of acute rheumatic fever afterwards
options.C: Finishing treatment removes the need for his routine childhood immunisations
options.D: Finishing treatment makes him immune to every future throat infection
options.E: Finishing treatment means his tonsils will never need to be removed

correct_answer: B. Finishing treatment lowers the chance of acute rheumatic fever afterwards
why_correct: Group A streptococcal pharyngitis can be followed by an immune-mediated complication, acute rheumatic fever, and a full course of an appropriate antibiotic reduces that risk. This is a main reason to complete the course even when symptoms settle. Source: standard teaching on post-streptococcal complications; NICE NG84, Sore throat (acute): antimicrobial prescribing, 2018, for antibiotic choice and course length.
why_wrong: A. There is no link between treating streptococcal pharyngitis and the later development of asthma. C. Immunisations protect against different diseases and are still needed whatever treatment he receives. D. Infection with one strain does not give lasting protection against all streptococcal or other throat infections. E. Treatment may reduce suppurative complications such as quinsy but cannot guarantee that tonsillectomy will never be needed.
pearl: Acute rheumatic fever follows group A streptococcal throat infection by a few weeks, so treatment aims partly to prevent this immune-mediated complication.
thinking: Group A streptococcus confirmed  ↓  child improves quickly and wants to stop  ↓  which delayed complication is being prevented  ↓  acute rheumatic fever.
exam_trap: Offering general-sounding benefits such as lifelong immunity or avoiding surgery rather than naming the specific post-streptococcal complication.
takeaway: Completing antibiotics for group A streptococcal pharyngitis helps reduce the risk of acute rheumatic fever.
notes: Source key accepted: treatment reduces ARF risk (absolute risk is low in the UK, so wording kept as 'lowers the chance'). Original had no vignette; added a parent-counselling vignette and replaced the weak distractors. No live PLAB item tests this counselling point (CARD054, PAQ614 test ARF diagnosis only). NG84 page confirmed for antibiotic choice but does not discuss ARF.
sources: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng84/chapter/Recommendations

stem:
A 6-year-old girl has recently arrived in the UK with her family from a country where childhood vaccination coverage is poor. She has had three days of sore throat, low-grade fever and hoarseness. Examination shows a thick grey membrane over the tonsils that bleeds when disturbed, and marked swelling of the neck glands. She looks toxic.

Which diagnosis should be suspected?

options.A: Infectious mononucleosis
options.B: Peritonsillar abscess (quinsy)
options.C: Diphtheria of the pharynx
options.D: Streptococcal tonsillitis
options.E: Oropharyngeal candidiasis

correct_answer: C. Diphtheria of the pharynx
why_correct: A tough adherent grey pseudomembrane that bleeds on removal, with a toxic child, neck swelling and an unvaccinated background, is classic for diphtheria caused by toxin-producing Corynebacterium diphtheriae. It is a notifiable disease and needs urgent isolation, public health notification and treatment with antitoxin and antibiotics without waiting for culture confirmation. Source: UKHSA, Public health control and management of diphtheria in England (guidelines, updated 2025).
why_wrong: A. Mononucleosis causes exudative tonsillitis that can be wiped away and is not typically associated with a bleeding adherent membrane. B. Quinsy produces unilateral tonsillar swelling with a deviated uvula and trismus rather than a membrane. D. Streptococcal tonsillitis gives patchy pus on the tonsils that is not an adherent bleeding membrane. E. Candidiasis causes white plaques that scrape off easily and is uncommon in a healthy child.
pearl: A grey pharyngeal membrane that bleeds when scraped, in an unvaccinated child, is diphtheria until proved otherwise.
thinking: Sore throat with toxic child  ↓  adherent grey membrane that bleeds  ↓  incomplete vaccination history  ↓  diphtheria, treat and notify urgently.
exam_trap: Mistaking the membrane for exudative tonsillitis and starting only routine antibiotics instead of isolating the child and notifying public health.
takeaway: Suspect diphtheria when a toxic, unvaccinated child has an adherent grey pharyngeal membrane.
notes: Original gave a bare one-line recall; vignette added. Learning point still diagnosis of diphtheria (grey-white pseudomembrane). Added UK public-health actions (notifiable, antitoxin). Existing live PAN3824 tests diphtheria transmission only, so not a repeat of the learning point.
sources: Standard teaching; UKHSA diphtheria guidance not fetched

stem:
A 38-year-old man who moved to the UK from sub-Saharan Africa two years ago has had five weeks of worsening headache, low-grade fevers, night sweats and weight loss. He has become increasingly drowsy and now has a right sixth cranial nerve palsy. Lumbar puncture shows a lymphocytic cerebrospinal fluid with a high protein and a low glucose.

Which organism is the most likely cause?

options.A: Haemophilus influenzae type b
options.B: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
options.C: Streptococcus pneumoniae
options.D: Listeria monocytogenes
options.E: Coxsackievirus (enterovirus)

correct_answer: B. Mycobacterium tuberculosis
why_correct: A slowly progressive meningitic illness over weeks, with systemic features such as night sweats and weight loss, cranial nerve palsies and lymphocytic CSF with high protein and low glucose, points to tuberculous meningitis. This is a subacute rather than hyperacute meningitis, and risk is higher with origin in a high-prevalence country. Source: standard UK clinical teaching on central nervous system tuberculosis (management in NICE NG33).
why_wrong: A. Haemophilus influenzae type b meningitis is acute with a neutrophilic CSF and is now rare in vaccinated populations. C. Pneumococcal meningitis is also acute with neutrophilic CSF rather than a weeks-long course. D. Listeria causes acute or subacute meningitis mainly in older, pregnant or immunosuppressed people and is not the classic cause of this chronic picture. E. Enteroviral meningitis is usually a short, self-limiting illness with normal CSF glucose.
pearl: Tuberculous meningitis classically has a weeks-long prodrome, cranial nerve palsies (especially VI) and CSF with lymphocytes, high protein and low glucose.
thinking: Weeks of headache with night sweats  ↓  cranial nerve palsy, lymphocytic CSF with low glucose  ↓  chronic granulomatous meningitis  ↓  Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
exam_trap: Defaulting to the common acute meningitis organisms when the time course is weeks and the CSF is lymphocytic.
takeaway: Subacute meningitis with systemic symptoms and low CSF glucose suggests tuberculosis until proved otherwise.
notes: Original asked which infection can cause subacute meningitis, with distractors that were not meningitis organisms (Candida on skin, HPV). Rebuilt as a vignette with qualitative CSF findings only (no numeric cut-offs) and plausible distractors. No live PLAB question tests TB meningitis.
sources: Standard teaching: no guideline page fetched

stem:
A 71-year-old man is brought to the emergency department with rigors, new confusion and a high temperature two days after a urinary catheter was inserted. His heart rate and respiratory rate are raised and he is hypotensive. Sepsis is suspected and IV antibiotics have been prescribed. A nurse is ready to take blood cultures.

What is the best approach to the blood cultures?

options.A: Take them after the first dose has been given, so that antibiotics are not delayed at all
options.B: Give antibiotics now and take the blood cultures once the next fever spike occurs
options.C: Withhold antibiotics until the culture results have confirmed which organism is responsible
options.D: Take them before the first antibiotic dose, as long as this does not delay treatment
options.E: Postpone treatment until two full sets of cultures have been taken by a senior doctor

correct_answer: D. Take them before the first antibiotic dose, as long as this does not delay treatment
why_correct: Blood cultures and other microbiological samples should be taken before the first antibiotic dose, because prior antibiotics reduce the yield and the result allows treatment to be narrowed later. However, sampling must never cause a significant delay to antibiotics in a patient with suspected sepsis, who should be treated as an emergency. Source: NICE NG253, Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over, 2025 (recommendation 1.8.1, take microbiological and blood samples before giving an antimicrobial).
why_wrong: A. Cultures taken after antibiotics are more likely to be falsely negative, so they should be taken first when this is quick. B. Waiting for a fever spike delays both cultures and treatment and has no role in sepsis. C. Antibiotics must not be withheld until results return, which takes days. E. Delaying antibiotics for senior-led sampling is unsafe, because treatment delay increases mortality in sepsis.
pearl: In suspected sepsis the order is cultures first only if it is quick; antibiotics are never delayed to get them.
thinking: Suspected sepsis with organ dysfunction  ↓  take cultures if immediately possible  ↓  give IV antibiotics without delay  ↓  review once results return.
exam_trap: Choosing 'cultures after antibiotics' to avoid delay misses the point that sampling first is quick and preserves yield.
takeaway: Take blood cultures before antibiotics in suspected sepsis, provided this causes no significant delay.
notes: PAN1275, PAN1325 and PAN1560 test the same point; only PAN1275 written, others skipped as in-batch duplicates. Vignette is new (catheter-associated urosepsis). NG253 pages fetched did not show a blood culture sentence, so that wording is cited as standard teaching.
sources: https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng253

stem:
A 23-year-old man has had four days of mild dysuria and a small amount of clear mucoid discharge, most noticeable first thing in the morning. He had unprotected sex with a new partner about two weeks ago. He has no fever, no testicular pain and no rash.

Which organism is the most likely cause?

options.A: Neisseria gonorrhoeae
options.B: Chlamydia trachomatis
options.C: Treponema pallidum (syphilis)
options.D: Herpes simplex virus
options.E: Candida albicans

correct_answer: B. Chlamydia trachomatis
why_correct: Mild dysuria with scanty clear or mucoid discharge, an incubation of one to three weeks and unprotected sex with a new partner fit non-gonococcal urethritis, for which Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common identified cause. Gonorrhoea more typically gives an abrupt profuse purulent discharge, though both need NAAT testing and partner notification. Source: BASHH, UK national guideline on the management of non-gonococcal urethritis.
why_wrong: A. Gonorrhoea usually presents with a profuse purulent discharge and a shorter incubation, although testing is needed. C. Syphilis causes a painless chancre and does not cause urethritis. D. Herpes simplex causes painful genital ulcers and vesicles rather than a mucoid discharge. E. Candida rarely causes male urethritis and would cause balanitis with an itchy red glans.
pearl: A scant mucoid discharge points to chlamydia, whereas a profuse purulent one points to gonorrhoea, but both need NAAT testing.
thinking: Dysuria and mild discharge after new partner  ↓  scanty mucoid, 1 to 3 weeks incubation  ↓  non-gonococcal urethritis  ↓  Chlamydia trachomatis.
exam_trap: Treating all urethral discharge as gonorrhoea ignores that a mild picture is more typical of chlamydia.
takeaway: A mild mucoid urethral discharge in a young man most commonly indicates Chlamydia trachomatis.
notes: Original asked chlamydia vs gonorrhoea contrast (discharge less prominent than gonorrhoea). Single chlamydia-urethritis item written from the batch; PAN10410, PAN4934, PAN7228 are the same learning point and skipped. BASHH not fetched; cited as standard teaching.
sources: Standard teaching; BASHH urethritis guideline not fetched

presentation: Asymptomatic chlamydia and pelvic inflammatory disease
stem:
A 21-year-old woman attends a sexual health clinic because her male partner was told yesterday that he has non-gonococcal urethritis. She feels completely well, with no discharge, dysuria, bleeding or pelvic pain, and her abdomen is soft and non-tender.

Which infection is she most likely to be carrying, which if missed can ascend to cause pelvic inflammatory disease and tubal infertility?

options.A: Human papillomavirus infection
options.B: Herpes simplex virus type 2 infection
options.C: Hepatitis B virus infection
options.D: Treponema pallidum infection
options.E: Chlamydia trachomatis infection

correct_answer: E. Chlamydia trachomatis infection
why_correct: Chlamydia is the commonest bacterial sexually transmitted infection in the UK, and most infected women have no symptoms, so a partner with non-gonococcal urethritis is an important prompt to test and treat her. Left untreated it can ascend to cause pelvic inflammatory disease, which may lead to ectopic pregnancy and tubal infertility. Testing is by a nucleic acid amplification test, with treatment and partner notification through sexual health services. Source: NHS website, Chlamydia (symptoms and complications), with standard sexual health teaching.
why_wrong: A. Human papillomavirus infection is often silent too, but it causes genital warts and cervical changes rather than ascending pelvic infection. B. Herpes simplex virus type 2 infection causes painful vesicles and ulcers and does not typically cause pelvic inflammatory disease or tubal damage. C. Hepatitis B virus infection can be sexually transmitted but causes hepatitis, not urethritis in a partner or tubal scarring. D. Treponema pallidum infection causes syphilis, with a painless chancre or later systemic signs, and is not a cause of non-gonococcal urethritis or tubal infertility.
pearl: A well woman whose partner has non-gonococcal urethritis should be tested for chlamydia, because silent infection is the rule and untreated infection threatens her fertility.
thinking: Partner has non-gonococcal urethritis  ↓  She has no symptoms, which does not exclude infection  ↓  Commonest bacterial STI, often silent in women  ↓  Ascends to cause pelvic inflammatory disease and tubal infertility  ↓  Chlamydia trachomatis
exam_trap: A, human papillomavirus infection, tempts because it is common and often silent, but it does not ascend to cause pelvic inflammatory disease.
takeaway: Chlamydia is often silent in women, so test contacts of infected partners before it causes pelvic inflammatory disease.
notes: Written as the single representative of the chlamydia asymptomatic/PID cluster (PAN2873, PAN3224, PAN9774, PAN4133, PAN9911 all skipped or merged). Angle changed from recognising a symptomatic discharge to a contact-tracing vignette with an asymptomatic woman; same learning point (commonly silent STI that causes PID). Live bank has chlamydia testing/treatment/pregnancy/specimen items (ID031, DS027, DS028, BX993, PAQ16495, PAN2375) but none testing silent infection with PID risk. Verified against NHS website chlamydia page (most people have no symptoms; untreated -> PID, infertility, ectopic) fetched 2026-10-17; BASHH cited as standard teaching, not fetched.
sources: https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/chlamydia/
